title: Scott v. Harris (2007)
summary: The majority treated the video as eliminating a genuine dispute about the danger of the chase; the dissent disputed that reading.
notes:
The casebook’s subsequent discussion reports research finding different viewer interpretations. That discussion is commentary on the decision, not part of the holding. No video is included in the uploads.

Harris sued under § 1983 claiming an unreasonable Fourth Amendment seizure after Deputy Scott rammed his bumper during a roughly ten-mile high-speed chase in Georgia, leaving Harris a quadriplegic; the Court ruled 8-1 in an opinion by Justice Scalia, with Justices Ginsburg and Breyer concurring and Justice Stevens dissenting.

Rule statement: when opposing parties tell two different stories and one is blatantly contradicted by the record so that no reasonable jury could believe it, the court should not adopt that version of the facts in ruling on summary judgment; the Court also held that an officer's attempt to end a dangerous high-speed chase by forcing the fleeing motorist off the road does not violate the Fourth Amendment even at risk of serious injury to the motorist.

sections.Parties: Harris, severely injured during a police pursuit, sued Deputy Scott for excessive force.
sections.Material Facts: Scott used his vehicle to force Harris’s fleeing vehicle off the road. Harris described the chase in a way that minimized the danger to others. An authentic, unaltered video in the record showed the pursuit. The parties’ different accounts made the video’s significance central to the qualified-immunity and summary-judgment dispute.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied summary judgment, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court reversed and held Scott entitled to summary judgment.
sections.Issue: Did the plaintiff’s account create a genuine factual dispute despite the video record?
sections.Holding: The majority held that it did not because the video blatantly contradicted the account of a safe or controlled flight.
sections.Reasoning: The Court reaffirmed favorable inferences for the nonmovant but applied that protection only to a genuine dispute. In its view, no reasonable jury could accept the account contradicted by the recording, and the danger justified the officer’s effort to end the chase. The evidentiary medium did not operate as a rule that all videos automatically control; the conclusion depended on what the majority believed this recording conclusively showed.

learning.why: The majority treated the video as eliminating a genuine dispute about the danger of the chase; the dissent disputed that reading.

topics.cp-inferences: The majority found that an undisputed authentic video blatantly contradicted the nonmovant’s account. Favorable treatment applies to genuine factual disputes, not an account no reasonable jury could accept.
topics.cp-judge-jury: The dissent disputed whether the video eliminated reasonable disagreement.
topics.cp-summary-judgment: Scott shows when a court may resolve a case on summary judgment despite the nonmovant's contrary sworn account.
topics.cp-frcp-56: The Court applied the Rule 56 genuine-dispute standard to a videotape in the record.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Stevens dissented, arguing that the video confirmed or at least permitted the lower courts’ interpretation and that the majority had displaced the jury’s role. Justices Ginsburg and Breyer wrote separately.
